extracted.intended_audience: policy officers and anyone involved in analysing, developing or implementing policy where regulation may be under consideration
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing, assessing and publishing Australian Government Impact Analyses (IAs): when an IA is required, the proportionality and content standards, the OIA assessment process (early and final two-pass), and transparency/publication and compliance requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Impact Analysis is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact Analysis is required for any policy proposal or action of government, with an expectation of compliance, that would result in a more than minor change in behaviour or impact for people, businesses or community organisations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation of compliance may arise from explicit obligations, industry-driven schemes (compulsory or voluntary), or inducements likely to change participant behaviour. Regulation affecting people/businesses outside Australia is in scope if there is also an impact in Australia. Agencies are responsible for ensuring IA requirements are met. Impact Analysis is not required for minor or machinery changes (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — Minor changes and Machinery changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor changes do not substantially alter existing regulatory arrangements; machinery changes are consequential changes required due to a substantive regulatory decision and often have limited discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of minor changes: online application process, indexation arrangements, setting opening/closing dates. Machinery examples: correcting legislative errors, administrative name changes, levy rate adjustments in line with CPI, updating fee thresholds. Some machinery changes may have significant impact but still be machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary Assessment requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to contact OIA early to confirm whether Impact Analysis is required for any policy proposal and any proposal proceeding to Cabinet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a written summary answering the seven Impact Analysis questions (use the 'Is Impact Analysis required?' template form if helpful). OIA will advise within five working days whether an IA is required and on the depth of analysis. Agencies can request carve-outs to avoid repeated preliminary assessments for routine minor/machinery changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key questions for Preliminary Assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: The key questions to answer when seeking a Preliminary Assessment: Who will be the decision maker? What is the policy problem? What are the objectives of government action? What policy options are available? What are the likely impacts of the proposal (including market or competition impacts)? What are the likely regulatory costs (administrative, substantive compliance and delay costs) as per the Regulatory Burden Measurement framework? What are the key dates and timelines?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide rudimentary answers early to enable OIA to advise on required depth of IA; OIA can workshop the policy process where time allows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The depth of analysis for the seven Impact Analysis questions is proportionate to the magnitude of the proposed change and the stage in the policy development process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key determinants: scale, scope and gravity of the problem; nature of the proposed intervention and alternatives and their potential impacts; stage of policy development and type of decision. Also consider the number of entities impacted, stakeholder interest, whether the proposal limits future options, distributional impacts and risk levels. Examples provided showing how proportionality applies to Cabinet vs non-Cabinet and minor vs significant proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum IA content by decision stage
rubrics_metrics.description: For a final policy decision: address all seven Impact Analysis questions in full. For earlier major policy decisions (subject to further consultation/decisions): at minimum address the first four Impact Analysis questions and provide a consultation plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An in-principle Cabinet decision to regulate or announcing an intention to legislate should be informed by a detailed IA that has completed at least the first four questions and provided an outline of consultation. Consulting without advocating a policy direction may require less detailed examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of impacts to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider direct regulatory impacts (e.g. compliance burden) and other significant flow-on impacts such as on the economy, competition, society, or the environment, including impacts on specific cohorts or market incentives/disincentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Regulatory Burden Measurement framework for regulatory costs but remember regulatory costs are often a subset of broader economic and other impacts; consider distributional impacts across gender, age, Indigeneity, disability, regions and small business where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Assessment and Final Assessment process
rubrics_metrics.description: OIA provides an optional Early Assessment and a mandatory Final Assessment. Assessments are undertaken only after the IA has been certified by your secretary, deputy secretary or chief executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early Assessment: once first four IA questions (including regulatory burden costing), consultation plan and certification are complete; focus on adequacy for consultation/initial decision and provide written advice. Final Assessment: two-pass process — first pass comments on consistency and completeness against seven questions; agency may revise; second pass relies on certification addressing OIA's comments; final IA then provided to decision maker and published after announcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-pass Final Assessment details
rubrics_metrics.description: Final Assessment is a two-pass process: first pass — OIA comments on whether the IA is consistent with requirements and sufficiently addresses the seven questions; second pass — OIA relies on the agency's certification letter (which must directly address OIA’s written comments) when determining adequacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may revise IA after first pass with no time limit and no limit on discussions with OIA. If OIA finds IA insufficient, agencies can still proceed to decision but OIA will provide written reasons. For Cabinet decisions, a copy of IA must accompany the submission unless OIA advises a summary is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIA assessment tiers and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: OIA categorises its assessment into Insufficient, Adequate, Good practice and Exemplary practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insufficient = poor quality process/analysis; triggers PIR requirement within two years. Adequate = sufficient for decision but contains shortcomings (e.g., consultation). Good practice = overall good quality addressing seven questions with only minor issues. Exemplary practice = exceptionally high quality analysis for each of seven questions and an exceptional process. Agencies should aim for exemplary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment — quality of analysis criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: OIA assesses whether the IA: simply and clearly explains the problem and objective; examines a range of viable, genuine policy options including non-regulatory; where fewer than three options feasible, explains why; analyses benefits and costs of all options in a balanced/objective manner; uses the most appropriate methodology considering strengths and limitations; quantifies regulatory impacts; shows distributional impacts; demonstrates meaningful consultation; recommends the option with the highest net benefit; includes a clear implementation and evaluation plan; describes the status of the IA at each major decision point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These items represent the substantive analytic standards against which the IA is judged. Where fewer than three options are presented, the certification letter must explicitly state and justify that circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment — quality of process criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: OIA assesses the policy development process: whether appropriate type/duration of consultation was undertaken; whether IA assessed by OIA was provided to decision maker prior to each major decision point; whether IA was certified by the secretary/deputy secretary/chief executive before formal OIA assessment; and whether where fewer than three options were considered the certification addressed this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of process can only lower the analysis rating (a good process does not raise a poor analysis). Process shortcomings (e.g., inadequate consultation) may move an otherwise strong analysis down a tier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to consider at least three policy options
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact Analysis needs to include at least three options unless the agency certifies that the policy problem and circumstances are such that fewer than three options are feasible. For election commitments and international agreements, fewer than three options may be acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If fewer than three options are presented, the IA should include a clear explanation why other alternatives are not viable or practical. OIA will expect the certification letter to explicitly state this where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Burden Estimate (RBE) and costing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: All proposals subject to Impact Analysis need to quantify the regulatory costs to people, business, and community organisations using the Regulatory Burden Measurement framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework guidance details how to quantify administrative, substantive compliance and delay costs, and how to identify offsets. Where a document is certified as an IA equivalent, regulatory costs must be calculated and set out in the certification letter. RBE tables (average annual impacts by people/business/community organisations) are used, including change in costs ($ million).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency — publication timing and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon announcement of a final decision, the IA provided to the decision maker will be published on the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet website, together with a one-page Impact Analysis Summary, the second pass certification letter and OIA’s written advice setting out the status of the IA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIA will obtain agency approval before publishing but aims to publish as soon as practicable after a final announcement. If no IA prepared or the published explanatory material does not match the IA assessed by OIA, OIA will make this clear. IA equivalents and supporting analysis are published with the certification letter. Draft IAs used to inform non-final Cabinet decisions must be finalised and assessed before a final decision; otherwise OIA will publish earlier IA and label the process insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on amending IA prior to publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in very limited circumstances, the IA submitted for Final Assessment and provided to the decision maker will be published and cannot be changed to support or justify the decision after the decision maker has made the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted limited changes (with OIA approval) include removal of commercial-in-confidence or national security info, correcting minor typographical/formatting errors without substantially changing meaning, adding relevant information that does not substantially alter analysis (e.g., consultation details or future reviews), and updating impacts where the decision maker modified the proposal. Failure to seek OIA approval for changes prior to publication will lead to an 'insufficient' report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addenda and post-publication additional information
rubrics_metrics.description: In limited circumstances, and with OIA agreement, agencies may publish an addendum to provide additional context or expand information after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addenda must be substantively similar to the original IA; material that would materially change the proposal requires a new IA and assessment. The original IA will remain unedited on the OIA website alongside any addendum. OIA will not formally assess addenda but may make general comments on quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of IA in explanatory memorandum or statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a regulation is tabled in Parliament, the IA (as assessed by OIA) needs to be included in the explanatory memorandum (for primary legislation) or explanatory statement (for legislative instruments) by default for non-minor/machinery IAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions (with OIA agreement) include when IA has been tabled previously with a stable link, or where IA is exceptionally long and a summary may be published instead. Agencies must seek OIA agreement to the exceptions before seeking Ministerial approval of the Bill. Failure to publish the IA in full without OIA agreement will be reported as insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and remediation when IA not exemplary
rubrics_metrics.description: If an IA does not achieve an exemplary rating, OIA will provide direction on improvements and communicate reasons. Where analysis is at the lower end of Adequate or at risk of Insufficient, OIA may meet or write, brief senior ministers, brief Cabinet through coordination comment, publish concerns, or assess IA as Insufficient (triggering PIR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should seek to address OIA concerns where practical. OIA will identify and communicate the reasons for not achieving exemplary status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of insufficiency — specific triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: An IA may be assessed as insufficient where: fewer than three options are considered without required certification; insufficiently articulating why the highest net benefit option was not selected; not conducting appropriate consultation; not sufficiently addressing the seven IA questions; or not sufficiently describing the IA status at each major decision point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An Insufficient assessment triggers a post-implementation review requirement within two years. Also, not providing approval to publish when required may lead to an insufficient report (but subsequent publication avoids PIR trigger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of compliance and OIA monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: OIA monitors regulations tabled in Parliament, news, media releases and other sources to identify decisions that may fall within the IA framework and will contact agencies if decisions appear to have been taken without required IA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After consultation, OIA will determine IA requirements have been met, process inconsistent (and publish reasons), or IA not met requiring a PIR and reporting the agency as insufficient. An agency's process may be deemed insufficient in Step 3 if it does not provide approval to OIA for publishing IA as soon as practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Web accessibility requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact Analyses and post-implementation reviews supplied for publication must conform to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2 (WCAG).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents must follow formatting/style conventions, and PDFs must have at least one alternative format (e.g., rich-text or HTML). Charts and tables may require extra work. Agencies should liaise with web services early; delays in providing accessible versions may attract a negative comment or an 'insufficient' assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carve-outs (standing agreements)
rubrics_metrics.description: OIA can grant a 'carve-out' — a standing agreement between OIA and an agency that removes the need for a Preliminary Assessment for minor or machinery changes that occur regularly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carve-outs improve efficiency while ensuring consistent advice about IA requirements; see Appendix 1 guidance note for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact Analysis Summary requirement (one-page)
rubrics_metrics.description: From August 2025 a one-page 'Impact Analysis Summary' approved at Deputy Secretary level (or equivalent) is required to be published on the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet website to complement Impact Analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Template for the summary is provided (link referenced). The summary accompanies the IA upon publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact Analysis equivalent processes
rubrics_metrics.description: If an Impact Analysis equivalent process has been undertaken by a department, agency, statutory authority, or board, agreement may be sought from OIA for that analysis to be lodged through the Impact Analysis equivalent process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact Analysis equivalents will be assessed by OIA for relevance to the recommended options; specific requirements are in the Impact Analysis Equivalent Processes Requirements guidance note. Where an IA equivalent is certified, regulatory costs must be set out in the certification letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-implementation reviews (PIRs) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: PIRs need to be prepared when decisions that fall within the IA framework have been taken without an IA, or when OIA assesses the IA as insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PIR must be completed within two years of implementation if IA was not prepared or was insufficient. For decisions assessed as having substantial or widespread impact on the Australian economy, a PIR needs to be completed and signed off by OIA within five years following implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cabinet submission IA input requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: All Cabinet submissions must meet the Australian Government Impact Analysis requirements. For proposals requiring detailed IA, attach the completed IA and include specified wording in the Impacts table. For proposals not requiring detailed IA, include comments in the Impacts table and an OIA ref ID.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where Cabinet is decision maker and IA is minor/machinery, IA requirements can be met by including a short statement in the Impacts table (Appendix 2 shows templates). IAs prepared for Cabinet decisions that are minor or machinery are not subject to formal assessment and are not published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor Impact Analysis — required content and template
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a Minor Impact Analysis is prepared (for proposals assessed as not requiring detailed IA), it should include: a summary of the proposed policy and any options considered; an overview of likely impacts; and an outline of regulatory costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Minor IA may be included in the Cabinet submission but is not formally assessed or published by OIA. A Regulatory Burden Estimate (RBE) table is used to quantify average annual regulatory impacts by people, businesses and community organisations (change in costs $ million). An example template and worked example are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinants OIA considers when advising depth of analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When advising on the depth of analysis, OIA takes into account a broad range of factors including level of difference from the status quo; number of entities impacted and degree of impact per entity; level of stakeholder interest and contest; whether the proposal limits future options; distributional impacts; and levels of risk involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These determinants inform the proportionality judgement and whether deeper analysis is required (e.g., for significant market interventions or measures likely to impose significant burden).
